options.text: English knowledge of Virginia's geography depended on information from Native peoples

options.misconception: The map's detail came from Native informants, not from an English survey of the whole region.
options.text: The English had already surveyed and mapped the entire Chesapeake by 1607

options.misconception: An inset portrait is not a treaty; Powhatan never agreed to English rule.
options.text: Powhatan had agreed to place his people under English rule

options.misconception: The map was made for English readers and investors, not for Native navigation.
options.text: The map was drawn to help Native peoples navigate English settlements

rationales.A: The map names dozens of Native towns, rivers, and peoples across a region the English had barely explored. Smith did not learn those names by walking the land himself; he learned them from Native guides, captives, and trading partners. The inset of Powhatan's court is the same story in miniature: the map's most striking details all come from the people the English had come to displace.
rationales.B: The map's detail came from Native informants, not from an English survey of the whole region.
rationales.C: An inset portrait is not a treaty; Powhatan never agreed to English rule.
rationales.D: The map was made for English readers and investors, not for Native navigation.
rationales.general:
1. Read the inset as a clue, not a decoration. It shows Powhatan's court — a world Smith entered as a prisoner, not a surveyor.
2. Ask where the names came from. Dozens of Native towns fill a region the English had barely walked.
3. Name the source of the knowledge. Native guides, captives, and trading partners supplied it.
Remember: when a map knows more than its maker could have learned alone, someone else taught him.

stimulus.text: John Smith's map of Virginia, published in 1612 and engraved by William Hole. Native towns and peoples are named across the whole map, and the upper-left inset shows Powhatan enthroned with his courtiers, captioned “Held this state & fashion when Capt. Smith was delivered to him prisoner 1607.” A Native man with a bow stands at the right, and the royal arms of James I sit at the center.
